Chapter 3: The Myth of “De Facto” Segregation.
Have you ever wondered why American neighborhoods are so divided? Most folks will tell you it comes down to personal choices—who could afford what, or maybe who wanted to live near whom. This idea, that segregation just sort of “happened,” is so common, hardly anyone stops to question it. But if you dig a little deeper, you’ll see the story just doesn’t add up.
Picture a teacher back in the 1950s, working in a city where schools are sharply divided along racial lines. She watches her students struggle—not because they aren’t trying, but because their neighborhoods are starved of resources. She hears parents talk about wanting more for their kids, but their options are so limited. Meanwhile, schools in white neighborhoods get new books, better buildings, and more experienced teachers. It’s not just about money—it’s about who’s even allowed to live in certain places.
The myth of “de facto” segregation says all of this is just the result of private choices, not government action. But the facts tell a different story. Time and again, it was government decisions that drew—and then reinforced—the lines that divide our communities. When Black families tried to move into white neighborhoods, they didn’t just face dirty looks or cold shoulders. They ran into legal barriers. Police were called—not to protect them, but to keep them out.
In many cities, local officials leaned on zoning laws to keep Black families out. They’d ban apartment buildings or require huge lots, making it impossible for anyone without a lot of money to move in. Sure, the rules didn’t mention race, but everyone knew what they were about. When someone challenged them, officials would talk about “protecting property values” or “preserving community character.” But the end result was always the same.
Banks and real estate agents played their part, too. They’d steer Black families away from white neighborhoods—sometimes refusing to show them homes, or quietly denying loans with no explanation. These practices—called “steering” and “blockbusting”—were illegal on paper, but happened all the time. What you ended up with was a housing market that looked fair and open, but really wasn’t.
The impact of all these policies reached way beyond just who lived where. For most Americans, owning a home is the main way to build wealth. By locking Black families out of the best opportunities, the government made sure that the gap between Black and white Americans would only get bigger, generation after generation. You can still see the effects today—in the wealth gap, in how schools are funded, even in health outcomes.
Most people don’t notice how these old policies still shape the world we live in. They see the neighborhoods, the schools, the jobs, but not the history that built them. The myth of “de facto” segregation is comforting because it lets everyone off the hook. But the truth? It’s more uncomfortable—and way more important. If segregation was made by policy, then policy can undo it, too.
